newsitem.title: USA: Jewell demands retractions by Atlanta papers.
newsitem.headline: Jewell demands retractions by Atlanta papers.

text.p: Former Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell has given Atlanta's two daily newspapers a week to retract a series of articles, which he says painted him as last summer's bomber.

In a letter accusing the Atlanta Journal and the Atlanta Constitution of publishing innuendo, Jewell attorney Lin Wood said the Cox-owned newspapers would have until next Wednesday to retract 20 "libelous" statements, in as conspicuous and public a manner as they first appeared.

The statements were excerpts from articles that ran in both papers over a three-day period from July 30 to Aug. 1 just after the bombing. The papers share their news staff and are known collectively as The Atlanta Journal-Constitution.
"The Atlanta Journal-Constitution ridiculed, accused and vilified an innocent man," Wood said in his letter, which he addressed to newspaper attorney Peter Canfield.
"The public justification offered by your client for its questionable ethics was a fear that it would have 'egg on its face' if scooped by another newspaper or a local television station."

Six of the allegedly libellous statements were taken from an Aug. 1 article that compared Jewell's story with that of Wayne Williams, the serial killer convicted in Atlanta's missing children cases of the early 1980s.
The others generally described Jewell as an avid publicity speaker who fit an FBI profile for the lone bomber.
Newspaper publisher Roger Kintzel said he stood by the accuracy of the stories.

Wood told Reuters his letter was intended to meet a state statute governing libel suits. Jewell will file a lawsuit against the Journal-Constitution and more than half a dozen members of its editorial staff by Nov. 20, he said.
Jewell's lawyers also have vowed to name NBC and its news anchor, Tom Brokaw, as defendants in a separate libel suit.

Jewell, 33, was working as a security guard near Centennial Olympic Park on July 27 when he spotted a suspicious-looking green knapsack at a crowded outdoor concert. He alerted police and helped to clear the area of concert-goers before a pipe bomb hidden in the knapsack exploded, leaving two dead and more than 100 wounded.

Initially, Jewell was hailed as a hero for his actions, but three days later an extra edition of the Atlanta Journal identified him as the focus of a massive bomb investigation. He spent the next 88 days as a virtual prisoner in his family's suburban apartment while a contingent of FBI agents and television camera crews camped outside.
His ordeal came to an end last month when the Justice Department publicly cleared him of suspicion in the case.
